title: Sender failed DMARC
lesson: A failed sender check means the message may be forged. If it claims to be from someone you know, confirm with them another way.

title: SPF or DKIM check failed
lesson: Real mail from a company is signed. Failed signatures are one more reason to slow down.

title: Replies go to a different domain
lesson: Look at where a reply would actually land. If it isn't the sender's own domain, the person writing may not be who they say.

title: Display name contains a different address
lesson: A name in quotes can say anything. The address behind it is the part that counts.

title: Display name poses as a brand
lesson: The name on a message is free text. Check the address, not just who it says it is.

title: Display name matches a protected person
lesson: Leaders get impersonated constantly. An odd request from the boss's name deserves a phone call, not a reply.

title: Free mailbox using an authority title
lesson: IT, payroll and HR don't write from free mailboxes. A title in the name proves nothing.

title: Talks as a brand, links nowhere near it
lesson: When a message says it's from a well-known company, go to that company's site yourself instead of using the link.

title: Fake reply thread
lesson: A subject starting with 'RE:' makes a cold message look like a conversation you've already had. Check for the thread.

title: Sender domain imitates a known domain
lesson: Read the domain letter by letter. Attackers register names that look right at a glance.

title: A link points at a lookalike domain
lesson: Hover before you click. The link's domain, not its text, tells you where you'll land.

title: Domain mixes alphabets
lesson: Some letters in other alphabets are identical to English ones. That 'a' might not be an 'a'.

title: Internationalised domain name
lesson: Domains starting with 'xn--' hide non-English letters. Be wary when one shows up in a message about your account.

title: Domain was registered very recently
lesson: Legitimate services have been around a while. A domain registered last week asking for a login is a red flag.

title: Link goes to a raw IP address
lesson: Real companies use names, not numbers. A link to an IP address is almost never legitimate.

title: Link text shows one site, link goes to another
lesson: What a link says and where it goes can differ. Hover to see the real destination before clicking.

title: Link hides its real host behind a login prefix
lesson: In 'paypal.com@other.example' everything before the @ is decoration. The site is what comes after.

title: Link is shortened
lesson: Short links hide where they lead. If you weren't expecting one, don't open it.

title: Link uses a high-abuse top-level domain
lesson: Some endings (.zip, .top, .click and friends) are cheap and heavily abused.

title: Link is on throwaway hosting
lesson: Free site builders are quick for attackers to spin up. A 'login' page on one is suspect.

title: Link runs script or embeds data
lesson: Links that start with javascript: or data: don't take you to a website. They run code.

title: Link bounces through several sites
lesson: Several redirects before the page appears is a way of laundering a bad link.

title: Link lands on a password form
lesson: A page that wants your password after you followed an email link should be treated as a trap. Go to the site directly.

title: Landing page uses a brand it doesn't own
lesson: A page can copy a company's look exactly. The address bar is the one thing it can't fake.

title: Attachment can run code
lesson: Files like .exe, .js, .iso or .lnk run programs. Real colleagues don't send those.

title: Attachment hides its real extension
lesson: 'invoice.pdf.exe' is a program wearing a PDF's name. Turn on file extensions and read to the end.

title: Attachment is a program disguised as something else
lesson: The file's contents didn't match its name. That mismatch is deliberate.

title: Attachment type doesn't match its name
lesson: A file whose contents don't match its extension is trying to get past a filter or past you.

title: Office file with a macro that runs on open
lesson: Never click 'Enable content' on a file you didn't expect. That button is how macro malware starts.

attack.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic

title: Office file contains macros
lesson: Documents that carry macros are rarely needed for ordinary business. Ask before opening.

attack.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic

title: HTML attachment
lesson: An HTML attachment is a web page that opens from your own computer. It's a common way to fake a login screen.

title: PDF with active content
lesson: A PDF should just be a document. One that launches things or runs scripts isn't.

title: Password-protected archive
lesson: Password-protected zips are a way to slip past scanners. A password sent in the same email is no protection at all.

title: Asks you to sign in, and fast
lesson: Pressure plus a login request is the classic pairing. Pause, then go to the site on your own.

title: Money request with warning signs
lesson: Requests to move money or change bank details need a second channel. Call the person on a number you already have.

title: Large amount of hidden text
lesson: Hidden text is there for scanners, not for you. It's a sign the sender is trying to look ordinary.

title: QR code in a short message
lesson: A QR code hides the link from filters and from you. Only scan codes you expected, and check where they go.

title: Password form inside the email
lesson: Real companies never ask for a password inside an email. If you see a login box here, it's a trap.

title: Generic greeting on an account message
lesson: Messages from a service you use usually know your name. 'Dear customer' is a tell.

title: Link is on a threat-intelligence list
lesson: This link is already known to be bad. Don't open it.

title: Attachment is known malware
lesson: This file's fingerprint matches known malware. Don't open it.
